History & Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
Young woman with no significant past medical history presents with an acute, left-sided throbbing headache that began at mid-day and was preceded by visual zig-zag aura; associated photophobia and two episodes of vomiting; exam details not documented, clinical impression is migraine with aura. She was counselled on analgesia use, headache diary, red-flag symptoms, and follow-up, with consideration of prophylactic therapy if headaches recur.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “terrible” left-sided throbbing headache since mid-day today.  
• Aura – Zig-zag lines and blurred vision in both eyes a few minutes before pain onset.  
• Course – Sudden onset; pain persists for several hours at time of consult; similar episode a few weeks ago lasted ≈2 days.  
• Modifying factors – Worse when leaning forward or moving head/neck; no specific relieving factor yet.  
• Associated symptoms – Photophobia (wearing sunglasses), nausea with two episodes of vomiting.  
• Review of systems / pertinent negatives  
  – No fever or chills.  
  – No skin rash.  
  – No speech difficulties, limb weakness, numbness, or balance/coordination problems.  
  – No breathlessness.  
  – No recent head trauma.  
• Prior headaches – Not usually headache-prone; one similar episode a few weeks ago.  
• Patient concerns – Fear of brain cancer due to friend’s family history.

Past Medical History:
• Denies chronic medical conditions.  
• No previous migraine diagnosis.

Medications:
• Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive pill) – dose/route/frequency not documented, in use for 3 months for contraception.  
• Occasional over-the-counter analgesics during prior episode (specific agents and dosages not stated).

Allergies:
• Not discussed / not documented.

Social History:
• Occupation – Works in the fashion industry; reports high job stress.  
• Living situation – Lives alone.  
• Exercise – None reported.  
• Tobacco – Denies smoking.  
• Alcohol – Denies alcohol use.  
• Recreational drugs – Not discussed.

Family History:
• Mother – Migraines and hypothyroidism.  
• No known family history of brain tumours.

Physical Examination:
(No objective examination findings recorded in transcript.)

Investigations:
• None performed or documented.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Suspected migraine with visual aura  
  • Assessment: Meets typical criteria (unilateral throbbing pain, visual aura, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, positive family history).  
  • Plan:  
    – Acute treatment: Paracetamol, or Co-codamol, and NSAID options (Ibuprofen or Naproxen); dose/route/frequency not documented.  
    – Non-pharmacologic: Rest in dark, quiet room; maintain hydration.  
    – Headache diary to identify triggers and frequency.  
    – Consider prophylactic migraine medication if headaches become frequent; discuss at follow-up next week.  
    – Safety-net: Return urgently if headache worsens, persists >2–3 days, medication ineffective, new focal neurologic symptoms, vision changes, or neck stiffness develop.

Issue 2 – Possible secondary headache (e.g., cerebral venous sinus thrombosis)  
  • Assessment: Moderate concern given recent initiation of estrogen-containing OCP and positional worsening; no focal deficits currently.  
  • Plan: Monitor progression; if headaches become persistent, atypical, or accompanied by neurologic signs, arrange urgent neuroimaging (MR venography) and blood work including coagulation profile.

Issue 3 – Health anxiety about brain tumour  
  • Assessment: Patient highly worried due to friend’s experience.  
  • Plan: Provided reassurance regarding current low likelihood; encouraged to re-present if red-flag symptoms develop; offered follow-up appointment next week for review and further discussion; consider stress-management strategies.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood. Classic unilateral throbbing pain, visual aura, photophobia, vomiting, family history, similar prior episode, absence of neurologic deficits.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Moderate likelihood. New severe headache, worsens on leaning forward, recent estrogen OCP use; lacks focal deficits but requires vigilance.  
3. Intracranial mass / brain tumour – Low likelihood. Positional worsening and vomiting could fit, but acute onset, lack of progressive course, and normal neurologic ROS argue against. No contradictions noted.

● Missing elements: Vitals, neurologic and general physical examination findings, allergies confirmation, full medication reconciliation, past surgical history.  
● Conflicts: None significant between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor conversational overlaps but clinically relevant information preserved.
